earthAtmosphere.title: Atmospheric Properties for Future Earth in Each of the 10 Scenarios
earthAtmosphere.transcriptionMethod: Manual transcription from the PDF table, checked against a rendered page and layout-preserving text extraction.
earthAtmosphere.nullSemantics: A null transcribes the table's ellipsis: the property is not listed for that case and must not be interpreted as numeric zero.
assumptions: All cases use a 1 bar background atmosphere composed of 78% N2, 21% O2, and 1% Ar.
The published global mean temperature assumes CO2 is the dominant greenhouse gas using Equation 1 of the source.
The source model atmosphere neglects changes to average water vapor and vertical atmospheric structure.
The table values are canonical inputs for generating modeled spectra; generated spectra are derived products.
notes: Stratospheric SO2 in S1, S2, and S6 represents solar-radiation modification.
Na emission represents high-pressure sodium lighting; S1 also includes directed laser emission.
S9 and S10 have the same listed Earth atmospheric properties as preagricultural Earth R0.
PSG spectra in Figures 1 and 2 do not include the listed Na or laser emission lines.
Every column descriptor and numeric/null table cell carries an exact table row/column locator.

venusAtmosphere.title: Atmospheric Properties for Future Venus in Each of the 10 Scenarios
venusAtmosphere.transcriptionMethod: Manual transcription from the PDF table, checked against a rendered page and layout-preserving text extraction.
venusAtmosphere.nullSemantics: A null transcribes the table's ellipsis: the property is not listed for that case and must not be interpreted as numeric zero.
assumptions: The grouped column S1-S4, S7, S8 applies identically to all six listed scenarios.
The table values are canonical scenario inputs; any spectra generated from them are derived model products.
notes: S5 and S6 involve ongoing terraforming by removing CO2 and SO2 while beginning to produce O2.
S6 and S9 use starshades to cool Venus.
S10 includes industrial floating cities that release atmospheric pollutants.
Every column descriptor and numeric/null table cell carries an exact table row/column locator.

collapse.title: Collapse-recovery model parameters and reported outcomes
collapse.transcriptionMethod: Parameters were transcribed from Table 4. Results include only values stated in prose or exactly defined by the paper; unreported chart-only values remain null pending digitization or author raw runs. Rendered pages 7 and 9-11 were visually checked.
assumptions: The paper describes 200 independent Monte Carlo simulations per scenario over 1,000 yearly time steps.
The result values are reported ensemble summaries, not independently reproduced simulation outputs.
A null result means no exact or safely rounded prose value was transcribed; it is not numeric zero.
notes: The paper's Code Availability statement on rendered page 20 links the author-hosted public repository https://github.com/celiablanco/technocycles. At audited commit 910770dbe9224a9f7b1e003fdc7c000c2d78a5c2, notebooks/figures.ipynb contains the simulation and figure code and initializes the main Monte Carlo generator with seed 12345; sensitivity batches use seed 54321.

The same commit contains notebooks/technosphere_summary.csv with aggregate results but no committed per-run trajectories. The repository declares no software or data license, so neither code nor CSV is ingested into canonical runtime data pending rights clarification.
This dataset therefore remains a transcription of the CC BY 4.0 paper; its result values have not been replaced by the unlicensed aggregate CSV.
Figure-only values are intentionally not guessed from bar heights.
Every simulation setting, parameter definition, scenario parameter, and reported-result field carries an exact source locator. Null figure-only outcomes carry resultCaptureStatus not_transcribed.
